2. Succinctly, the facts of the case, as stated in the writ petition, are that three groups of people, claiming themselves as the owners of the three different pieces of land, mutated their respective lands vide three Mutation cases namely, Mutation Case No. 4191 of 2011-2012 dated 15-3-2012, Mutation Case No. 5825 of 2011-2012 dated 11-6-2012 and Mutation Case no. 5824 of 2011-2012 dated 11-6-2012. While the writ petitioner's right, interest and claim, conjointly with that of respondent Nos. 8-10, lies in Mutation Case No. 5825 of 2011-2012, Mutation Case No. 5824 of 2011-2012 is with regard to the record of right of respondent Nos. 6 & 7 and Mutation Case No. 4191 deals with the record of right of respondent No.11. After coming to know about the above records of rights in the names of the above three sets of people, respondent No. 5 together with other two persons complained to the Assistant Commissioner (Land), Chandpur (hereinafter referred to as the A/C Land) on 17-1-2013 that the names of the petitioner and respondent nos. 6-11 (for ease of reference the petitioner and respondent nos. 6-11 hereinafter would be treated as one group and referred to as "the petitioners", given that their interest is same and they seek the same remedy) have been wrongly mutated and thus, prayed for reviewing the order passed by him in the aforesaid mutation cases. Pursuant to the said objection, the above three Mutation Cases were reheard upon being registered as Review Case No. 154 of 2012-2013 and by order dated 10-6- 2013 the A/C Land upon hearing both the sides cancelled the earlier mutations recorded in the names of the petitioners. The above U-turn stance of the A/C Land in disposing of the Review Case No. 154 of 2012-2013 prompted the petitioners to prefer an appeal before the appellate authority namely, Collector of Chandpur (respondent No.2) who allocated the same for disposal by respondent No. 3 who upon hearing both the parties allowed the appeal vide order dated 13-8- 2013. Against the said order dated 13-28-2013 respondent no.5 filed an application before respondent No.2 who asked respondent no. 3 to deal with the matter. Then, pursuant to an order passed by respondent No. 3 on 1-9-2013 the impugned order has been issued by the Officer-in- Charge of the office of respondent No. 2 and, hence, this Rule. 

 7. He candidly maintains that apparently though the petitioner could have invoked the appellate forum before the Divisional Commissioner, however, since the petitioner believes that respondent no. 3 does not have any jurisdiction to review his own decision, his approaching before this forum is a correct step. In an endeavour to simplify this point, he submits that he has considered writ jurisdiction to be an efficacious forum given that the Divisional Commissioner is not competent to interpret the legal provisions relating to appeal, revision and review as set out in the SAT Act. He argues that the Divisional Commissioner would not have been in a position to undertake an examination as to whether review is exercisable only at the original forum by the A/C Land or the same is also available at the superior-level authority. By making the aforesaid submissions the learned Advocate for the petitioner prays for making the Rule absolute. 

 17. The second component of section 147 is that the order should be passed "by a Revenue officer" in order to qualify an order to be appealable or to come within the purview of appeal. Revenue officer has been defined in section 2(24) in the following terms "any officer whom the Government may appoint to discharge all or any of the functions of a Revenue-officer under this Act or any rules made thereunder". Since it is apparent that the Assistant Commissioner (Land) and all other upward-ranking authority, including the Members of the Board of Land Administration, have been appointed by the Government to perform some functions under the provisions of the SAT Act, they are to be regarded as 'Revenue Officer's . 

 (4) The Board of Land Administration may at any time order the correction of any entry in a record-of-rights maintained under this Part or in a settlement rent-roll prepared and finally published under this Part which, it is satisfied, has been made owing to a bona fide mistake: 

 28. In the case of Amir Khan vs Controller of Estate Duties 13 DLR (SC) 105 it was held that the Court can modify the language to give effect to the manifest and undoubted intention of the Legislature. 

 31. In the case of Attorney General vs Lockwood (1842) 9 M &W 378 it was held that where the language of a statute, in its ordinary meaning and grammatical construction, leads to a manifest contradiction of the apparent purpose of the enactment, or to some inconvenience or absurdity which can hardly have been intended, a construction may be put upon it which modifies the meaning of the words and even the structure of the sentence. 

 33. In the case of Tirath Singh vs Bachiltar Singh AIR 1955 SC 830 the Indian Supreme Court viewed that where the language of a statute, in its ordinary meaning and grammatical construction, leads to a manifest contradiction of the apparent purpose of the enactment, or to some inconvenience or absurdity or hardship or injustice, presumably not intended, a construction may be put upon it which modifies the meaning of the words and even the structure of the sentence. 

 38. In performing the functions of legal interpretation, this Court is required to minutely read through the ambiguous provisions concurrently with the other provisions in the same chapter on top of grasping the scheme of the law and, then, give a word/phrase appropriate meaning with sound reasoning. 

 44. The crucial issue to be taken into consideration by the Judges in this kind of situation with great care is whether they are attaching a different meaning to the provisions in course of performing the functions of interpretation. Here, if we read the word as "confirming" In section 150(2) of the SAT Act, the provisions of section 147 of the SAT Act shall be inconsistent to the second part of the provisions of 150(2) of the SAT Act inasmuch as appeal will lie against an order reversing the previous order passed by the A/C Land in his review jurisdiction. Thus, by attributing the said meaning, we are not transgressing into the domain of the Legislature, rather we are performing our functions of interpreting the law which we are oath bound to do. 

 48. The apparent reason behind not making any provision putting restrictions on the power of revisional or review authority, as has been imposed in the authority of the civil revisional or review Courts, are that the general people are not acquainted with the technical and limitational factors attached to the legal parlance of appeal, revision and review and they should not suffer for failing to select the appropriate route of law. All that a layman understands is that when an authority rejects his case, he should be allowed to approach the higher authority. Our above view would not seem to be inconceivable if anyone seeks to be familiar with the background-history and the scheme of the SAT Act. In a nutshell, however, it can be said that the said law was enacted for the well being of the peasants who were being humiliated by the Zaminders for decades. Therefore, keeping this aspect in view, for the interest and benefit of the commoners the Legislature has kept open and flat provisions for all the jurisdictions namely, appeal, revision and review empowering all the said authorities to deal with every aspect of a mutation case, including legal and factual issues, ignoring the necessity of framing rules or setting up separate guidelines for three different fora so that they may be able to avail a next forum in the event of their dissatisfaction with the order of the original Revenue Officer. At the same time, the Legislature was also cautious to specify the two different routes, namely, the appellate route and the route of review, in order to save the simple-hearted citizenry of this part of the world from being unnecessarily harassed by encountering the situation of 'sort of double jeopardy' by the unscrupulous litigants and their cohorts. 

 52. From our scrutiny, it reveals that usually all the Collector Offices of our country use a pamphlet-type notice containing both the words "appeal" with a slash "revision", which appears in the said notice as আপীল/রিভিশন Therefore, the said move by the petitioners before the Collector is to be treated as revision in the backdrop of the operation of the words "appeal shall lie from every original or appellate order ". There is nothing to be prejudiced by the petitioners for treating the said move as "revision" instead of an "appeal" inasmuch as the extent of the powers, of the concerned authority, sitting in both the capacity, namely appellate or revisional, are same in entertaining the said second-tier move by an aggrieved party. In other words, when a Collector is approached by an aggrieved party against an original order of the A/C Land, the move shall be termed as an appeal and if it is against the A/C Land's order of review, it shall be termed as a revision and the remedy that will be provided to the aggrieved party by the Collector shall be the same since no different modus operandi will be applied in presentation of the aggrieved party's case and in conducting the hearing and pronouncement of the orders, irrespective of terming the move by the aggrieved party as an appeal or revision. 

 59. Both the sides are, thus; at fault in choosing the appropriate forum and it is apparent that it happened due to the absence of any Rule outlining the guidelines as to which order is appealable and which one is revisable. In view of the fact that the specification of the two routes of the Mutation Cases was not done previously by the Executives or was not available in any judge-made law, we hold that none of the parties are to be held liable for having failed to approach the right forum, rather due to the petitioner's present move, this Court had an occasion to lay down the appropriate guidelines. Given the above scenario of this case, the present Rule should be disposed of with the following directions upon the concerned authorities of the country. 

 (iv) The Board of Land Administration, however, shall be competent to order the correction of any entry at any time in presence of all the claimants of the land, if it finds any bona fide mistake in a finally published record-of-rights or in a settlement rent-roll.
